first.rationale: Onboarding completion is down 4% QoQ, directly matching the problem space where memory_86 and memory_31 showed durable gains. Verifying memory_86 (shortening onboarding lifted adoption) and memory_73 (promotional pricing effectiveness) is strategically important: memory_86 directly supports the intended action and carries high consequence; memory_73 represents the competitive threat but may be tactically premature given the activation problem predates competitive pricing pressure. Simplify_onboarding addresses root product engagement metrics (completion and activation) rather than masking them with pricing, aligns with sustainable long-term revenue (memory_86 showed durable lift, not just acquisition), and can be validated quickly in a small_guarded_test before full rollout. This preserves the option to pivot to promotional_pricing if onboarding simplification fails to move activation metrics, while addressing the more fundamental engagement decline.

final.rationale: Verification confirms memory_86 is reliable: shortened onboarding produced +13% completion, -2.1 day time-to-value, and critically +3% 30-day retention—a genuine durability signal. This directly addresses the 4% onboarding completion decline. Memory_73 verification revealed a critical failure mode: promotional pricing acquired customers at +31% but lost them at renewal (−12% 30-day retention). This eliminates promotional_pricing as a sustainable response to competitive pricing pressure and reinforces that discounting the wrong cohort destroys long-term value. Given the primary objective is sustainable long-term qualified revenue, not short-term acquisition, simplify_onboarding is the clear choice. The 6% activation decline and 4% completion decline are mechanically linked—shortening the onboarding path reduces friction and abandonment, improving both metrics. Scale to standard_experiment (not broad rollout) to measure impact on activation directly before full deployment, reducing execution risk on a time-sensitive metric.
